name: American persimmon
scientific: Diospyros virginiana. Two other persimmons are wild in the US and both are edible — black-fruited Texas persimmon (D. texana) in central and west Texas, and naturalised Japanese persimmon (D. kaki) at old homesites through the Southeast — so 'persimmon' on a Texas or Gulf-coast map does not always mean this tree.
habitat: Two quite different places, and the one that feeds you is the open one. Persimmon grows largest on alluvial terraces and river bottoms — clays and heavy loams, wet flats, shallow sloughs and swamp margins — but it is also the classic weed tree of worn-out ground, taking abandoned pasture, fencerows, roadsides, powerline cuts, old homesteads and dry sandy or gravelly uplands where little else will hold. It is very shade tolerant and will sit in a bottomland understory for years without fruiting: the trees that actually carry fruit are the ones standing in light, so work edges, field margins, fencerows and lone trees in the open rather than closed canopy. It suckers from the roots into clonal thickets and it is dioecious — only female trees fruit, and an entire thicket can be one male clone and therefore barren for good. Range is southern Connecticut and Long Island south to southern Florida, west through southern Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to southeastern Iowa, and south through eastern Kansas and Oklahoma to the Colorado River valley in Texas; 'northeast' here means southern New England and the mid-Atlantic, not northern New England, and there is no wild persimmon in the Rockies or on the West Coast. Habitat can NEVER be used to rule out either of the deadly lookalikes. Chinaberry holds the identical fencerows, roadsides and old homesites through the southern half of that range, and hangs its fruit on bare branches in exactly the same months. And buckeye drops its capsules onto the same ground in the same weeks all across that range — Ohio buckeye in the midwestern river valleys, ravines and low-woods edges, yellow buckeye in the Appalachian coves and bottoms, red buckeye as an understory shrub of woodland edges and naturalised ground through the Southeast and south-central states, and horse chestnut planted at the very yards and old homesteads this entry sends you to first. Finding a fruit on the ground in good persimmon habitat proves nothing whatever about what that fruit is. Habitat does not identify a fallen fruit. Cutting it open does.
indicator: Old-field succession on tired upland soil — eastern redcedar, sassafras, winged elm, sumac and broomsedge taking back a worn-out pasture, with persimmon usually in that group and often the only thing in the fencerow still holding fruit after leaf drop. In the bottoms, look on the low terrace just above the sweetgum-and-sugarberry flats. On the ground in October, opossum and raccoon scat packed with big flat seeds says a fruiting female is within a short walk; the trunk confirms it — thick dark bark broken into small square blocky plates, like alligator hide.
parts: Fully ripe fruit only, and ripe means jelly-soft: skin translucent and wrinkling, deep orange to reddish, the whole fruit collapsing under light thumb pressure, the four-lobed calyx peeling back and letting go. Ripe fruit is usually already on the ground. Firm fruit is not ready even when it is fully orange. BE CLEAR WHAT THAT SOFTNESS IS AND IS NOT: it is a ripeness test and it is never an identification. A green Aesculus capsule — buckeye or horse chestnut — dents under the thumb exactly like a ripening persimmon, and buckeye drops on the same ground in the same weeks at overlapping size, so no fruit is a persimmon because it felt soft. The thumb tells you whether a persimmon you have already identified is ready to eat, and tells you nothing at all about what species you are holding. See the buckeye lookalike and the fruit check in the harvest note for what actually settles it. Astringency tracks ripeness, not cold — Purdue Extension states outright that the fruit does not have to experience a frost to ripen; frost merely arrives at the same time of year, and a tree dropping sweet fruit in Alabama in late September has never seen one. Unripe fruit is loaded with soluble tannin (shibuol), which is not just unpleasant: in stomach acid it polymerises into a hard coagulum, and persimmon is the textbook cause of the diospyrobezoar, a mass that can obstruct the stomach or bowel and often needs endoscopic or surgical removal. Reported cases usually involve eating a lot of persimmon, skin on, on an empty stomach; prior gastric surgery, diabetic gastroparesis and low stomach acid are the recognised risk factors. No cooking or leaching is required for safety — ripening is the preparation. Fruit picked slightly firm will often come round in a closed paper bag with a ripe apple or banana at room temperature over 3–7 days, or after 24–48 hours in the freezer followed by a slow thaw; fruit picked hard and green usually just rots without ever sweetening, so do not treat either method as a rescue for bad picking. Peel, or push the pulp through a food mill or colander: the skin carries the most tannin, each fruit holds up to eight flat seeds the size of a thumbnail, and blending the seeds turns the pulp bitter. Eat one or two and wait before committing to a bucket, and do not put away a large quantity of even fully ripe fruit at a sitting on an empty stomach. This entry covers the fruit only.

lookalikes.name: Buckeye and horse chestnut (Aesculus glabra, A. flava, A. pavia, and naturalised A. hippocastanum)
lookalikes.tell:
THE GROUND-GATHERING TRAP, AND THE REASON THIS ENTRY IS RATED EXPERT TWICE OVER. This entry tells you to gather windfalls, and a fallen fruit has no leaves attached to read — so the tell has to live in the fruit itself. Buckeye lands on exactly the ground persimmon does, in exactly the same weeks: Ohio buckeye (A. glabra) fruits September–October in midwestern river valleys, ravines and the edges of low woods; yellow buckeye (A. flava) holds the Appalachian coves and bottoms; red buckeye (A. pavia) runs as an understory shrub of woodland edges and naturalised ground through AL, AR, FL, GA, IL, KY, LA, MO, MS, NC, OK, SC, TN, TX, VA and WV — essentially the whole southern and central half of persimmon's range; and horse chestnut is a standard planting at the yards, farmsteads and roadsides this entry names first. Habitat and calendar cannot separate them.

SIZE DOES NOT CLOSE IT EITHER. Persimmon fruit is 0.8–2 in. An Aesculus capsule is 1–2.25 in in A. glabra, 1.5–2 in in A. flava and 1–3 in in A. pavia — the ranges overlap outright, and a big persimmon and a small buckeye capsule are the same object at arm's length. Size is a filter, not a verdict. Nor does spininess: the capsule is prickly in A. hippocastanum, warty-prickly in A. glabra, and perfectly smooth in A. flava and A. pavia, so a smooth husk proves nothing.

AND NEITHER DOES FIRMNESS — THIS IS THE THING TO UNLEARN. A green Aesculus capsule dents under thumb pressure exactly as a ripening persimmon does. 'Jelly-soft' is how you know a persimmon is ready; it is not how you know it is a persimmon. Never let a fruit into the bucket because it felt soft.

THREE CHECKS THAT DO WORK ON A FRUIT IN THE HAND. (1) THE CALYX. Persimmon keeps a leathery four-lobed calyx clamped at the stem end and usually comes off the tree with it still attached, with a small beak (the dried style) at the other end. An Aesculus capsule has no calyx whatever — just a bare stalk scar. (2) THE SEAMS. A buckeye capsule shows three seams and parts along them into three tidy valves as it dries. A persimmon has no seams and never splits that way; an overripe one tears open irregularly and weeps orange pulp, which is a different thing and is fruit you were going to discard anyway. (3) CUT IT THROUGH — the decisive check, five seconds, one fruit. Persimmon is thin smooth skin over abundant soft orange pulp holding up to eight flat brown seeds the size of a thumbnail. An Aesculus is a thick leathery rind that peels off one to three smooth, shell-less seeds the blade drives straight into as solid ivory — glossy mahogany when ripe, pale ivory when green, each with one big pale scar — with no pulp, no flat seeds and no smell. A ripe persimmon smells sweet; an Aesculus capsule has no fruit smell at all, scratched or whole. Never taste to decide.

OVERHEAD, WHEN THERE IS A TREE TO READ. Every Aesculus has OPPOSITE, PALMATELY COMPOUND leaves — five to seven leaflets spreading from a single point on one stalk, like fingers from a palm. Persimmon leaves are simple, alternate, oval, untoothed and dark glossy, and its mature bark is thick and broken into small square blocky plates like alligator hide. There is no overlap and no exception: compound opposite leaves overhead means walk away from the fruit under it.

NC State Extension rates A. flava, A. pavia and A. hippocastanum Poison Severity: High — of red buckeye 'Highly toxic, may be fatal if eaten', of yellow buckeye that it can cause death in humans, livestock and pets, of horse chestnut 'HIGHLY TOXIC, MAY BE FATAL IF EATEN'. The toxic principles are the glycoside aesculin and the saponin aescin, in seed, fruit, leaf, bark and stem: vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, muscle weakness, dilated pupils, twitching, incoordination, paralysis and stupor. The National Capital Poison Center records severe poisoning after as few as one to four seeds. No Aesculus seed is edible by any preparation, and historical accounts of buckeye eaten after prolonged leaching are not a procedure to attempt. For any suspected ingestion call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222). Rule: identify the tree by its leaves, or cut the fruit open. Colour and squeeze are not identification.

lookalikes.name: Chinaberry (Melia azedarach)
lookalikes.tell: The second thing here that can kill you, and the one that exploits the exact cue that makes persimmon easy to find — small orange-tan fruit hanging on a bare tree in a fencerow after the leaves are down. Chinaberry fruit persists through fall, winter and into spring, shrivelling to wrinkled yellow-tan, in the same roadsides, thickets, field edges and old homesites. Tells that work on the fruit in hand, in the season you are picking: chinaberry drupes are 0.4–0.5 in (1–1.3 cm) and hang in loose drooping clusters of many fruits on a branched stalk, while persimmon fruit is 0.8–2 in (2–5 cm) and borne singly (occasionally two or three) close against the twig. Ripe chinaberry has no calyx; persimmon keeps a leathery four-lobed calyx clamped at the stem end and usually comes off the tree with it still attached. Break one open — chinaberry is thin sticky mucilaginous flesh over a single hard, round, ridged stone; persimmon is abundant soft orange pulp around up to eight large flat brown seeds. Whole-tree tells: chinaberry leaves are enormous (12–24 in) and twice-pinnately compound with toothed leaflets, against persimmon's simple, oval, untoothed, dark glossy leaves, and persimmon bark is thick and blocky in small square plates. Note that chinaberry's leaves are ALTERNATE and twice-pinnate while buckeye's are OPPOSITE and palmate — two different deadly trees, two different leaves, and neither is persimmon's simple oval. Toxicity is tetranortriterpene (limonoid) neurotoxins concentrated in the fruit: most US poison-centre exposures are young children and stay minor, but human poisoning is documented at roughly six to nine fruits — vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, weakness, seizures, respiratory distress, paralysis — and deaths are reported in the clinical literature. Where the published tell fails: chinaberry is a warm-climate naturalised tree, running roughly from Virginia and southern Maryland south through Florida and west through Oklahoma and Texas, with scattered outliers further north. Through the Midwest and Northeast it is effectively absent, so this is a Southeast and south-central risk rather than a range-wide one — which is a reason to be sure of your latitude, not a reason to relax where it grows, and note that buckeye covers the northern ground chinaberry does not. For any suspected ingestion call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) rather than waiting for symptoms.

lookalikes.name: Horsenettle, tropical soda apple and climbing nightshade (Solanum carolinense, S. viarum, S. dulcamara)
lookalikes.tell: Round yellow, orange or red berries in the same abandoned pastures, fencerows and roadsides, ripening and persisting through the same autumn months, all carrying solanine-type glycoalkaloids: burning mouth, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and with a real dose drowsiness, confusion and slowed breathing, with children the usual casualties. The structural tell holds all season and needs no flowers: these are herbs and vines, never trees. Horsenettle is a knee-high prickly herb with lobed, star-shaped leaves and spines on stem and leaf midribs, its smooth yellow berries 0.4–0.6 in shrivelling on the dead stalk into winter. Tropical soda apple (Florida and the Gulf states, especially pasture) is a viciously spiny herb 3–6 ft with mottled green fruit ripening yellow at about 1 in. Climbing nightshade is a twining vine through fencerow brush with red ovoid berries under 0.5 in. In every case the berry is thin-skinned with dozens of tiny flat seeds in wet pulp, sitting in a green star-shaped calyx; persimmon is a soft 0.8–2 in berry on a woody tree with up to eight large flat brown seeds and a leathery four-lobed calyx.

lookalikes.name: Oriental and American bittersweet (Celastrus orbiculatus, C. scandens)
lookalikes.tell: Not something you would gather off the ground on purpose, but it is what most often pulls a beginner across a field in November, and it is the one lookalike that can end up in your container without you walking to it: a woody vine climbing into a fencerow tree — very often into the persimmon itself — hung with orange-yellow fruit on bare stems long after leaf fall. Shake that tree and bittersweet lands on your sheet with the persimmons, so sort the sheet by hand. In hand there is no ambiguity. Bittersweet fruits are 0.25–0.35 in capsules packed in clusters along the stem, each splitting into three orange-yellow valves that expose a scarlet fleshy aril; persimmon is a single soft berry 0.8–2 in with a four-lobed calyx and never splits. The berries cause vomiting and diarrhoea and are implicated in more serious poisoning in children, usually via dried ornamental wreaths. Before you walk to a tree, check what is holding the fruit — a woody twig or a twining vine.

lookalikes.name: Japanese / Oriental persimmon (Diospyros kaki)
lookalikes.tell: Harmless in itself, but it teaches the wrong lesson. Planted throughout the Southeast and persisting for decades at old homesites — precisely where wild persimmon also grows — with fruit 2.5–4 in, often flattened or acorn-shaped, few or no seeds, a large four-lobed calyx spreading flat like a saucer, and much larger, broader leaves than the native. Non-astringent cultivars (Fuyu type) are eaten crisp and hard, so anyone whose only persimmon experience is a supermarket Fuyu will bite a firm native and get a mouthful of tannin they will not forget. Astringent cultivars (Hachiya type) must go completely jelly-soft exactly like the native, and D. kaki is the species behind most published bezoar cases, so it carries the same load. The rule for anything in this genus that is not a known non-astringent cultivar: soft or nothing.

lookalikes.name: Hardy orange / trifoliate orange (Citrus trifoliata, syn. Poncirus trifoliata)
lookalikes.tell: A naturalised hedge shrub of Southeastern fencerows, old homesites and woodland edges that drops golf-ball-sized downy yellow-orange fruit in the same weeks persimmon drops, into the same grass. The fruit settles it instantly: hard, dry and dense, covered in fine fuzz, unmistakably citrus-scented when scratched, with a thick pithy rind over sour segmented flesh and many plump seeds — persimmon is soft, smooth-skinned and pulpy with flat brown seeds. The plant settles it from twenty feet: hardy orange carries stout green thorns 1–2 in along green twigs and three-parted leaves. Note that hardy orange's three leaflets are ALTERNATE and its twigs are green and thorny, where buckeye's five to seven leaflets are OPPOSITE on a thornless twig — do not let 'compound leaves' collapse the two together. Not poisonous, just ferociously sour and mostly pith — and the thorns will punish a hand pushed into the thicket.

harvest:
Gather windfalls. Shaking or picking firm fruit only gets you astringent fruit and wastes it, and a single tree ripens over three or four weeks, so the method that works is returning to the same tree every few days through the drop rather than clearing it once. Shake only if the fruit still hanging is already jelly-soft, lay a sheet if you do, and expect to sort.

RUN THE FRUIT CHECK BEFORE ANYTHING GOES IN THE BUCKET. Gathering windfalls is exactly where the buckeye mistake happens, and no leaf tell can save you on the ground — a fallen fruit has no leaves attached to read — so the check has to live in the fruit itself. For every fruit you did not personally watch come off a persimmon-leafed twig: it must be 0.8–2 in, round, thin-skinned and smooth, not a 1–3 in globe or pear with a thick leathery rind; it must still carry the leathery four-lobed calyx clamped at the stem end, where an Aesculus capsule has no calyx at all and only a bare stalk scar; and it must show no seams, because a buckeye capsule parts along three clean seams into three tidy valves while a persimmon has none. Do not sort by squeezing. A green buckeye capsule dents under the thumb exactly like a ripening persimmon, so firmness is a ripeness test and never an identification. Then cut one through as a positive check: cut the first fruit of the day as a matter of course, and cut any fruit you are the least unsure of. Persimmon is thin skin over abundant soft orange pulp holding up to eight flat brown seeds the size of a thumbnail; a buckeye is a leathery rind peeling off one to three smooth seeds that the blade drives straight into as solid ivory, with no pulp and no flat seeds. If a single fruit does not cut like a persimmon, cut the rest one at a time or tip the whole bucket out — and never mill, mash or pulp fruit you have not opened and looked inside.

THE SHEET GETS THE SAME TREATMENT, and it catches more than the tree you shook. Bittersweet climbs up into fencerow persimmons, so a shake drops its 0.25–0.35 in three-valved orange capsules with scarlet arils onto the sheet along with the fruit; a chinaberry or a buckeye standing over or beside the tree will drop onto it too, and windfalls already lying on the ground land under whatever else overhangs them. Sort the sheet by hand and let nothing through that is not 0.8–2 in, calyx-on, soft and single.

Sort on the spot: keep fruit that is soft, whole and smells sweet, and leave anything split and weeping, sour or alcoholic-smelling, fuzzy with mould, or busy with fruit flies — persimmon on the ground ferments fast, which is what the drunk-opossum stories are about — then rinse what you keep before it reaches the kitchen.

Late fruit is a southern tail, not a season. The peak drop is September through November across the cited range, which is what this entry's months show; NC State does record fruit displaying into December and hanging on the tree after the leaves are down, and a mild-winter tree in the Deep South can still be carrying sweet fruit then. Treat anything you find that late with more suspicion, not less: December sits deep inside chinaberry's persistence window, when its shrivelled yellow-tan drupes hang on bare branches in the same fencerows and there are no leaves left overhead to tell the two trees apart. The cluster, calyx and cut-open checks above are the whole of your protection once the canopy is gone.

Mind where you pick: persimmon's favourite ground (fencerows, roadsides, railroad rights-of-way, old farmsteads) is also the ground most likely to be sprayed or to carry historical pesticide residue, so stay well back from road surfaces and off anything under a spray programme. The species is not scarce, but it is a keystone autumn food — opossum, raccoon, grey and red fox, coyote, white-tailed deer, wild turkey and black bear all live on it through the fall, and it shows up in their scat all season — so clear part of the drop under any one tree and move on rather than stripping it. Remember the tree is dioecious and root-suckering: only females fruit, a whole thicket can be one barren clone, and a reliable female is worth knowing, protecting and not over-picking. Ask permission on land you do not own; many state parks and public lands limit or prohibit collection.

name: Bull Kelp (Bullwhip Kelp)
scientific: Nereocystis luetkeana (Mertens) Postels & Ruprecht. The genus is monotypic — there is exactly one Nereocystis, so a correct genus call is a correct species call, which is unusual comfort in this guide. The common name is far less stable: "bull kelp" means Durvillaea antarctica in New Zealand and Chile and is loosely applied to Laminaria and Saccharina in the North Atlantic, and Alaskan "ribbon kelp" usually means Alaria marginata, not this plant. Match the binomial, not the name on the sign.
habitat:
Cold, clear, moving seawater over hard bottom. The holdfast has to grip bedrock or a boulder big enough not to roll, so a bull kelp bed marks rock even when the rock is invisible from the surface — that is the single most useful thing the canopy tells you. Beds form on subtidal reef, headlands and channel edges from roughly 10 to 70 ft (3–20 m), deeper where the water is clear, and they want current or tidal surge to keep nutrients moving without the full shock of the outer wave-swept zone — that band belongs to sea palm and the stiff-stiped Laminaria setchellii and Pterygophora. It needs full-strength cold seawater: bull kelp thins out in brackish river plumes and in the warm stratified water south of Point Conception. Under the canopy sits the usual understory — Laminaria, Pterygophora, Costaria, Agarum, coralline crust, red and purple urchins — and on top of it, sea otters, harbour seals and gulls.

Range is Pacific salt water and nothing else: from about San Luis Obispo County and Point Conception in central California north through Oregon, the Washington outer coast, the Strait of Juan de Fuca, the San Juans and Puget Sound, up the British Columbia coast into Southeast Alaska, the Gulf of Alaska and west along the Aleutians. None of that maps onto an inland region, so read the "west" tag as the saltwater edge of the west and no further.

The biological fact that matters most to a forager: Nereocystis is an ANNUAL. Each plant germinates from a microscopic overwintering gametophyte in late winter, races to the surface in one season at up to about 4 inches a day, releases spores, and is torn out by the first autumn storms. A bed you cut last July may simply not be there this July, and a bed can fail outright after a warm winter or once urchins move in. Between 2014 and 2017 more than 90% of the bull kelp canopy along 217 miles of northern California went to urchin barrens and has not returned; Puget Sound has lost most of its historic South Sound beds. Treat a healthy bed as scarce, not as scenery.
indicator: A line of fist- to grapefruit-sized amber floats lying over a rocky reef with blades streaming away downcurrent. At slack low water the whole bed goes flat and points where the ebb went — which is also the only hour it is sane to be inside it in a kayak. Sea otters rafting in the canopy, or gulls standing on it, mark a bed dense enough to be worth the paddle. On the beach, a wrack line of intact whips with the holdfast still clenched around a fist of rock means the bed is close inshore and shallow.
parts:
Blades, stipe and bulb are all edible, and none of it is toxic raw — every bit of cooking below is for texture, iodine or bacteria, never for detoxification.

Blades are the beginner's part and, in Washington, the only part the law leaves you on a living plant: olive-to-golden straps 3–6 in wide and up to 10–15 ft long, hanging in a terminal cluster of thirty to sixty from the top of the float. Take young, unfouled, sweet-smelling ones. Rinse in clean seawater, then blanch 30–60 seconds in boiling water — they flip to a startling bright green — and use them in salads, soups and stir-fries, or dry them hard and grind them as a seasoning. Late-season blades carry a white lacy crust (the bryozoan Membranipora) and fuzzy hydroid growth: scrape those off or leave the blade, because the hydroids sting the mouth and the crust is grit.

The hollow stipe and the bulb are the pickling parts — peel the tough brown outer skin down to pale flesh, slice into rings, pickle. Two hard rules. First, kelp is a low-acid food and cannot be safely water-bath canned unless the recipe is properly acidified: use a tested recipe built on 5%-acidity vinegar in enough volume to hold the finished jar below pH 4.6, or skip canning entirely and keep them as refrigerator pickles eaten within a few weeks. Never store kelp under oil. Clostridium botulinum is the specific organism and botulism is fatal. Second, mussels, barnacles and other filter feeders settle on the stipe and holdfast, and in Washington, British Columbia and Alaska those animals carry paralytic shellfish poison — saxitoxin, of which about one milligram can kill an adult, and which is destroyed by neither cooking, freezing nor pickling. Strip every attached animal off before the stipe goes in the pot, and never eat one because it came up with the kelp.

Iodine is the quiet dose problem. Kelps commonly exceed 1,000 µg of iodine per gram of dry weight and the adult tolerable upper intake is 1,100 µg per DAY, so a single dried gram can put you over it. Treat dried bull kelp as a seasoning, not a vegetable. A water blanch strips out most of the iodine into the discarded water — published trials on sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) removed the large majority of it that way — so blanch before drying if you plan to eat it often. Anyone with thyroid disease should talk to a doctor before making kelp a habit.

The harmless confusions are worth naming so you stop worrying about them: giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera, which carries a small float at the base of EVERY blade rather than one big one at the top), feather boa (Egregia menziesii), winged kelp (Alaria marginata), sugar and sea-cabbage kelps (Saccharina, Hedophyllum) and rockweed (Fucus) all share the water and are all edible. Getting one of those instead of bull kelp costs you texture, not health.

lookalikes.name: Acid kelp / witch's hair / sea sorrel (Desmarestia ligulata, D. viridis, D. aculeata)
lookalikes.tell: THE TELLS THAT MATTER ARE BLADE TELLS, because the published tell for bull kelp — one hollow whip, one round float — is useless the moment the blade is cut free or drifting, which is how most of this gets picked. On the blade itself: a bull kelp blade is an unbranched strap, 3–6 in wide, smooth, with NO midrib and no side branches, olive-brown to gold, and it stays firm, glossy and slick for hours. Desmarestia ligulata is a flattened blade with a distinct midrib running its whole length and opposite side-branchlets coming off it — branching alone rules bull kelp out. D. viridis and D. aculeata are fine, stringy, bushy and feathery, yellow-green to olive, nothing like a strap but very easy to scoop out of drift. The behavioural tell is the reliable one: Desmarestia bleaches to a sickly pale yellow-green within minutes to an hour out of water, goes slack and sour-smelling, and starts to dissolve. It holds sulfuric acid in its vacuoles at an internal pH around 0.5–0.8. Foraging and phycological sources agree it is not poisonous and will not kill you — it tastes viciously acrid, stings eyes and broken skin, and the operational damage is that ONE frond will acidify and digest every other blade in your bag within a couple of hours. It grows and drifts at the surface in the same beds right through bull kelp season, so this is a summer problem, not a theoretical one. Bag drift species separately, and throw out anything that has been sitting next to it.

lookalikes.name: Surfgrass (Phyllospadix scouleri, P. serrulatus, P. torreyi) and eelgrass (Zostera marina)
lookalikes.tell: These are flowering plants, not algae, and they are the commonest thing tangled through a wrack line with cut kelp. Hold a blade to the light: surfgrass and eelgrass show PARALLEL VEINS running the length of the leaf and a true sheath at the base; a bull kelp blade has no veins at all. Colour and width settle it too — surfgrass is bright grass-green and only 2–4 mm wide, eelgrass bright green and 2–12 mm, while bull kelp blades are 3–6 in across and olive to golden brown. Pull one up in place and eelgrass comes out of sand or mud on a white creeping rhizome with true roots, and surfgrass is combed flat over wave-swept low-intertidal rock. Neither will poison you; both are tough, fibrous and not food. The reason this matters is legal, not medical: recreational take of Zostera and Phyllospadix is prohibited outright in California and in Oregon.

lookalikes.name: Wireweed / Sargassum (Sargassum muticum throughout, S. horneri in southern California)
lookalikes.tell: This is the trap for anyone who has reduced bull kelp to "look for the float." Sargassum carries MANY floats — pea- to marble-sized, each on its own short stalk, scattered along a much-branched stem with small leaf-like blades. Bull kelp has exactly ONE float per plant, fist- to grapefruit-sized (up to about 6 in), sitting at the top of a single unbranched hollow stipe with all the blades springing from the float itself. If the piece in your hand branches, it is not bull kelp. Rockweed (Fucus) is the same mistake in miniature: paired swollen bladders at the tips of a forked, flattened, midribbed frond. S. muticum is abundant on rock and cobble in Puget Sound, the San Juans, Oregon estuaries and California bays, often in exactly the water you are working. Neither will poison you — they are simply tough and disappointing — but taking one home means you never actually learned the mark, and the mark is what keeps Desmarestia out of the bag.

harvest:
Bull kelp is habitat — for rockfish, herring spawn, juvenile salmon, otters — before it is food, and the rules across its range are stricter and far more varied than most foragers assume. Take blades from many plants rather than stripping one, never touch or lift the holdfast, and prefer fresh drift: a whip that came in on the last tide, still cold, firm, slick and sweet-smelling, is as good as a cut one and costs the bed nothing. Kelp on the beach that has gone slack, warm, brown-slimy or ammonia-smelling is compost, and eating it is how people actually get sick from this plant.

Washington: a Shellfish/Seaweed licence or combination fishing licence is required; 10 lb wet weight per person per day (RCW 79.135.410); knife or similar instrument only, no tearing and no rakes or forks; the anchor point stays in place; and bull kelp must be cut AT LEAST 24 INCHES ABOVE THE BULB (12 inches above the anchor point for short-stemmed kelps). Read that literally — the bulb sits at the top of the stipe and the blades come off above it, so on a living Washington plant you may take blade tissue only, leaving the float, stipe and holdfast whole. Pickled stipe and bulb have to come from drift, or from another state. Harvest is limited to state-owned aquatic lands and to private tidelands with the owner's permission, and is closed in many state parks and marine preserves.

Oregon: living seaweed on the ocean shore is governed by Parks and Recreation, not ODFW — one gallon per person per day, three gallons per calendar year, individual containers with no combining, hand or knife only, no removing or disturbing a holdfast, and a season of 1 March to 15 June ONLY. That window shuts before the bull kelp canopy is properly up, so in Oregon the summer canopy is effectively look-don't-cut; non-living drift may be collected year-round. Eelgrass, surfgrass, sea palm and listed species are off limits, as are the marine reserves.

California: a sport fishing licence is required; 10 lb wet weight per day in the aggregate across all marine algae; eelgrass (Zostera), surfgrass (Phyllospadix) and sea palm (Postelsia palmaeformis) may not be taken at all; and take may be prohibited in state marine protected areas, marine recreational management areas, state marine parks and special closures. Given the >90% canopy collapse from Sonoma north, the honest advice on the north coast is to leave it entirely alone.

Alaska: rules differ again and personal-use seaweed harvest is more permissive — check current ADF&G guidance, and check DEC's water-quality and biotoxin picture for the specific water you are cutting in.

Everywhere: this is cold moving water with boat traffic in it. Work a slack low tide, wear a PFD, and do not swim into a bed — the stipes are strong enough to hold a boat and strong enough to hold you. Stay well clear of harbours, marinas, industrial shorelines and sewage outfalls; kelp sits at the surface and takes on whatever the surface is carrying.

name: Beach plum
scientific: Prunus maritima Marshall — no meaningful synonymy problem; the only infraspecific taxon you will meet is var. gravesii (Graves' beach plum), a round-leaved dwarf known from a single Groton, Connecticut population and legally protected. The common name travels, though: 'beach plum' is used in Florida for cocoplum (Chrysobalanus icaco) and on the Pacific coast for osoberry / Indian plum (Oemleria cerasiformis), and Great Lakes 'beach plum' is planted P. maritima on restored dunes. This entry is the Atlantic dune shrub, Maine to Virginia.
habitat: Deep, coarse, excessively drained sand with almost no organic matter — a full-sun pioneer that tolerates salt spray, burial by blowing sand and long drought, and tolerates neither shade nor wet feet. Look on the landward slope and back side of stabilised foredunes, in the hollows and secondary ridges behind them, on sandy bluffs and headland edges, and inland on old sand plains, sandy roadsides and the open fringe of pitch-pine barrens. There is no canopy over it by definition: as pitch pine and scrub oak close in over a stabilising dune, beach plum thins and disappears within a couple of decades, so healthy stands sit in the open band between the beachgrass and the woods. It suckers from the roots, so bushes come in clones and one good patch is often one plant — which is also why a whole patch can ripen on the same day while a clone fifty yards on is two weeks behind. Constant companions: American beachgrass (Ammophila breviligulata) seaward; bayberry (Morella pensylvanica), beach heather (Hudsonia tomentosa), bearberry, dewberry, poison ivy and Virginia creeper in the same thicket; Rosa rugosa, greenbrier and pitch pine landward. Range is coastal New Brunswick and Nova Scotia through Maine (rare and state-listed there), all of southern New England, Long Island, the New Jersey shore, and Delmarva to Virginia's Eastern Shore and barrier islands. That Virginia limit is the whole southern story, and it is why this entry carries no Southeast tag: in this guide Delaware, Maryland and Virginia all sit inside the Northeast region, and the Southeast region begins at North Carolina — which is where beach plum stops. Records from the Carolina Outer Banks south are plantings, dune-restoration escapes, or a different plant under a borrowed name; on a Florida or Gulf beach 'beach plum' means cocoplum, not this. Critically: standing in coastal sand rules nothing out. Virginia creeper grows through beach plum thickets on essentially every stabilised dune in the range, pokeweed stands in the blowouts, path edges, parking-lot margins and beachfront hedgerows from Cape Cod to Virginia, privet and buckthorn own the back-dune scrub and old hedgerows, inkberry holds the coastal-plain sand from Cape Cod south, cherry laurel is planted around beach houses the length of the coast, and Go Botany records Canada moonseed as disjunct on Cape Cod. Habitat can never be the argument.
indicator: The open shrub band on the landward side of a stabilised dune — beachgrass below it, bayberry and beach heather beside it, pitch pine behind it. Thigh-high bayberry with bare sand showing between the clumps is the signature; beach plum is usually in that band, wind-sheared flat across the top at whatever height the salt burn allows. The surest way to find it is to scout in flower: for roughly ten days in early to mid May (late April on Delmarva, into early June downeast) the dune thickets go white with blossom on bare grey twigs before a single leaf opens, and nothing else on the dune does that. Mark those bushes and come back in September.
parts: Ripe fruit, and nothing else on the plant. Fruit is 1/2–1 in across, dull purple-blue under a heavy waxy bloom (yellow, crimson and near-black forms turn up on the same dune), borne singly or in pairs on short stalks directly along grey woody twigs, with ONE flattened almond-shaped stone inside yellow-green flesh. Leaves are alternate, simple, elliptic, 1.5–3 in, finely toothed the whole way round, dull above and paler and often slightly hairy beneath. Ripe means it gives slightly under the thumb and releases with a gentle twist; hard, tight-skinned or red fruit is not ready and is astringent past use. Across the range, expect first pickings in the first half of August on Delmarva and the Jersey shore, peak in September everywhere, and fruit into the first half of October in Maine and the Maritimes. The flesh is tart and very high in pectin — pleasant raw when dead ripe, but this is a jelly, jam and syrup fruit. SAFETY PREPARATION IS ABOUT THE STONES AND ABOUT WHAT ELSE IS IN THE BUCKET. As in every Prunus, the stones, leaves, twigs and bark carry cyanogenic glycosides (amygdalin) that release hydrogen cyanide when a kernel is crushed and wetted; the flesh does not and needs no cooking, leaching or special handling. Cooking whole fruit with the stones in is standard and safe: simmer 10–15 minutes to burst the skins, then push the pulp through a food mill or china cap that holds the whole stones back, or drip it through a jelly bag. Never run beach plums through a blender, food processor, stick blender or seed-cracking mill, and discard any batch in which stones were shattered. Do not brew leaves or twigs, and do not add cracked kernels for almond flavour. Sort the bucket before it reaches the pot — a creeper, pokeweed or privet berry cooked into jam is undetectable. If canning, half-pint jars of finished jam or jelly go into a boiling-water bath for 10 minutes; beach plums are picked at sea level, so no altitude adjustment applies.

lookalikes.name: Virginia creeper (Parthenocissus quinquefolia)
lookalikes.tell: THE REALISTIC FAILURE MODE IS NOT MISIDENTIFYING A BUSH — IT IS PICKING BY THE HANDFUL OUT OF A TANGLE. Creeper grows over and through beach plum thickets on stabilised dunes across the entire range and ripens at exactly the same time, so its berries end up in the bucket, then in the pot, where nothing is recoverable. The plant: a woody vine with tendrils tipped in adhesive pads, and palmately compound leaves of five toothed leaflets radiating from one point on a single stalk — beach plum leaves are simple, alternate and finely toothed, on a self-supporting shrub. The fruit, which is what you must actually judge: 1/4–3/8 in, dull blue-black, in a branched cluster on stalks that turn coral-red to magenta in autumn, versus beach plum's larger fruit sitting singly or in pairs on short stalks straight off grey woody twigs, never on a red-stalked branching cluster. Do not lean on the red stalks in August — early in the season the cluster stems are still green and the leaves hide the fruit entirely, and the colour tell only becomes obvious around leaf drop. The decider once fruit is in your hand: cut it. Creeper has 2–4 small hard seeds in thin watery greenish pulp; a plum has one flattened stone. NC State Extension rates it poison severity High: "May be fatal if fruit is eaten," from oxalate raphides and probably more — abdominal pain, bloody vomiting, diarrhoea, dilated pupils, sweating, weak pulse, facial twitching. Documented human deaths are few and mostly historical, but the rating stands and children are the ones at risk. Sort every bucket berry by berry.

lookalikes.name: Pokeweed / pokeberry (Phytolacca americana)
lookalikes.tell: THE COMMONEST WRONG BERRY IN A BUCKET ANYWHERE IN THE EAST, and the dune is no exception. It stands in blowouts, on path and parking-lot edges, in the disturbed sand behind the primary dune, along sandy lanes and through every old beachfront hedgerow from Cape Cod to Virginia — which is precisely the ground this entry walks you across — and it carries ripe dark purple-black fruit from August into October, the entire beach plum season, with no window where one is out and the other in. Nothing on it is woody. It is a herbaceous perennial 4–10 ft that dies to the ground every winter: one thick, smooth, hairless stem you can cut with a thumbnail, no bark, no grey twigs, no spur shoots. A beach plum is a woody, wind-sheared shrub anchored in sand. Do not lean on the famous red stem — pokeweed stems are green well into summer and redden as the season goes, so a green-stemmed plant in August proves nothing. Fruit architecture settles it in one look: a pokeberry is glossy rather than bloomed, about 1/4–3/8 in (to 3/4 in), flattened top and bottom and ribbed into roughly ten segments like a miniature pumpkin, with a small green star of sepals on top, and dozens of them hang on individual short stalks along ONE long unbranched drooping raceme 4–8 in off a stem tip. A beach plum is 1/2–1 in, dull under a heavy waxy bloom, sitting singly or in pairs on a short stalk straight off grey woody twigs, never on a hanging raceme. Cut one: a pokeberry holds about ten hard, flat, lens-shaped black seeds in a ring in soft pulp; a plum has ONE thick flattened almond-shaped stone. Crushed pokeberry runs strong magenta-crimson and stains permanently. All parts are toxic — root worst, green berries worse than ripe — from the saponins phytolaccatoxin and phytolaccigenin plus a mitogenic lectin: burning mouth, cramping, violent vomiting, foamy or bloody diarrhoea and low blood pressure two to six hours after eating, with seizures and respiratory failure in bad cases. Poison centres put a serious dose for a child at about ten berries, and deaths are on record. The whole risk is that you are pulling handfuls rather than looking at single fruits, and a pokeberry cooked into jelly is undetectable — sort the bucket berry by berry. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) rather than waiting to see.

lookalikes.name: Canada moonseed (Menispermum canadense)
lookalikes.tell: A twining vine — no tendrils, no adhesive pads — with large 4–8 in leaves that are broadly heart-shaped to shallowly 3–7 lobed with a SMOOTH, untoothed margin and a stalk attached just inside the leaf edge rather than at the notch. Nothing about the foliage resembles beach plum's small, finely toothed, alternate leaves on a woody shrub. The fruit is the problem: dull blue-black with a bloom, about 1/3 in, ripening August into September in a loose branched hanging cluster, and it is the classic deadly wild-grape lookalike. The standard grape tell also separates it from plum, but you have to read it correctly: moonseed's single seed is a thin flattened disc notched into a crescent or ring, and its pulp is scant and bitter; a plum stone is a thick, plump, hard, almond-shaped pit filling the fruit. 'One seed' alone is NOT the tell — the shape is. On range, be honest with yourself: moonseed is mostly a plant of moist woods, thickets, streambanks and fencerows inland, and it is uncommon on the outer coast, but Go Botany records it as disjunct on Cape Cod, which is the busiest beach-plum ground in the country, and it climbs into shrub thickets on the back side of dunes and along sandy lanes. Dauricine and related alkaloids; ingestion has been fatal. Do not pick from a tangle by feel, and do not let a vine draped over a plum bush go unlooked-at.

lookalikes.name: Cherry laurels — Carolina laurelcherry and English laurel (Prunus caroliniana, planted P. laurocerasus)
lookalikes.tell: SPLIT OUT OF THE WILD-PLUM GROUP ON PURPOSE, BECAUSE IT DOES NOT BELONG THERE. Every other Prunus below trades you flavour; this one is graded with the killers, in line with the rest of this guide. These are the evergreen laurels — Carolina laurelcherry wild and self-seeding through the southern coastal plain and planted well north of it, English laurel planted as hedging and foundation shrubs around beach houses, motels and parking lots the entire length of the range, and both bird-sown from there into back-dune scrub and old beachfront hedgerows. The leaves settle it in every month including harvest season: thick, stiff, leathery, glossy dark EVERGREEN blades 2–6 in, untoothed or with a few scattered sharp teeth, on a dense shrub or small tree that holds its foliage all winter. Beach plum is deciduous, with thin, dull, finely toothed 1.5–3 in leaves on a low wind-sheared dune shrub that stands bare from November to May. The fruit tells you too: small shiny black drupes about 1/3–1/2 in in short clusters, almost entirely stone under a thin bitter film of flesh, held on into winter — not a soft juicy 1/2–1 in plum under a heavy waxy bloom that ripens and drops. WHY THIS IS DEADLY AND NOT MERELY BAD-TASTING: cherry laurel is the extreme of Prunus cyanogenic chemistry. Leaves, seed and green stems are loaded with prunasin and amygdalin — crushed P. laurocerasus foliage smells strongly of bitter almond and was the standard entomologist's killing-jar plant precisely because it gives off hydrogen cyanide — and the flesh is so scant that eating the fruit means eating the stone. Laurel foliage and clippings are a documented killer of livestock, poisonings of children who have chewed the leaves are on record, and 'laurel water' distilled from the leaves is a historical poison. No ripeness, no cooking, no milling step makes any of it safe. Never put cherry laurel fruit in the pot, never brew or chew the leaves, never let hedge clippings near the kitchen. Leave the plant alone entirely.

lookalikes.name: Chokecherry and black cherry (Prunus virginiana, P. serotina)
lookalikes.tell: Graded deadly here for the same reason this guide grades them deadly elsewhere: the flesh is traditional food, and the whole danger is in how whole fruit gets processed. Both reach the coast — black cherry is a common tree of maritime forest, back-dune woods and beachfront hedgerows the length of the range, and chokecherry is a thicket shrub of the same edges — so a bucket filled fast in mixed scrub can carry them. Fruit alone decides it at arm's length: chokecherry and black cherry hang twenty to fifty small fruits, each roughly 1/4–3/8 in, along a single central axis in a long cylindrical raceme 2–6 in long. Beach plum bears fruit 1/2–1 in singly or in pairs on short stalks directly off grey twigs, and never in a raceme. Leaves separate them too — chokecherry is abruptly short-pointed with sharp outward-pointing teeth, black cherry has blunt incurved teeth, a strip of rusty-brown hair along the midrib beneath and a pair of small red glands on the leaf stalk at the blade — and snapping a twig gives bitter almond, which beach plum does not. Where this turns dangerous rather than merely disappointing is the pot: a cherry stone is small enough to pass a food mill or be shattered by a blender, stick blender or seed mill, while a beach plum stone is big and flat and gets held back — and a crushed cherry stone releases hydrogen cyanide from amygdalin. Children have been poisoned and have died after eating large quantities of whole chokecherries, seeds included, and wilted Prunus leaves are the classic livestock killer on the same chemistry. Swallowing an intact stone is generally harmless (Poison Control); crushing one is not. If cherries are in the bucket, pit them or pick them out — never grind, never blend, and discard any batch in which stones were shattered.

lookalikes.name: Privet — border, common and California (Ligustrum obtusifolium, L. vulgare, L. ovalifolium)
lookalikes.tell: The most abundant black-fruited shrub in old beachfront hedgerows and back-dune scrub from Massachusetts to Virginia — planted for a century, now naturalised through exactly the thickets you are picking. Leaf arrangement decides it any month there are leaves: privet leaves are OPPOSITE, in pairs directly across from each other, small, untoothed and glossy; beach plum leaves are alternate and toothed all round. On fruit, in season: privet berries are hard, dull blue-black, under 1/4 in, in dense branched clusters at the TIPS of the twigs, and they hang on all winter — beach plum fruit is larger, soft and juicy at ripeness, single or paired along the twig, and gone by November. Cut one: 1–4 seeds in scant green pulp, no stone. NC State Extension rates fruit and leaves medium severity, with glycosides including syringin — abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, drooling, diarrhoea, weakness, low blood pressure and cold clammy skin that can run 48–72 hours; death is listed as possible but rare. Children have needed hospital care from a small handful of berries.

lookalikes.name: Common buckthorn and glossy buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica, Frangula alnus)
lookalikes.tell: Big invasive shrubs to small trees of coastal thickets, dune edges, swales and roadsides through the northern half of the range. This is the arrangement match that matters: pea-sized round black drupes, ripe from late August into September, in small tight clusters in the LEAF AXILS along the twig — the same position as a beach plum. Checks that work while the fruit is on the plant: common buckthorn leaves are sub-opposite with 3–5 pairs of veins that curve strongly forward and run parallel to the leaf margin toward the tip, and most twigs end in a short sharp thorn; glossy buckthorn leaves are glossy, untoothed, with 8–9 pairs of nearly straight veins. Beach plum has alternate toothed leaves with straight veins ending in the teeth. Do not settle the question on thorns — old beach plum spur shoots go stiff and stubby and read as spines to a beginner, so thorniness is not a reliable separator either way. Cut the fruit: buckthorn has 3–4 hard angular seeds and juice that stains purple-black; a plum has one flattened stone. Anthraquinones and emodin make it violently cathartic — cramping and watery diarrhoea to the point of dehydration, which is why its old use as a purgative was abandoned. One honest caveat, from UMN Extension's work: emodin levels drop sharply as the fruit ripens and little or none is found in fully ripe R. cathartica, so 'the ripe ones are milder' is technically true and completely useless. You will still be ill, and there are other irritants in it.

lookalikes.name: Inkberry and other hollies (Ilex glabra, I. opaca, I. verticillata, I. vomitoria)
lookalikes.tell: Inkberry is the one that genuinely shares the sand: an evergreen shrub of coastal-plain sand, dune swales and pine-barren fringe from Cape Cod to Virginia, with round black fruit under 1/4 in sitting singly in the leaf axils — the same size, colour and position as a small beach plum. The leaves settle it in every month of the year, including harvest season: thick, leathery, glossy, EVERGREEN, with a few blunt teeth only near the tip; beach plum is deciduous with thin, dull, finely toothed leaves. The fruit is hard and dry rather than juicy and stays on the bush through winter. Cut it: 4–7 small hard nutlets, no stone. Saponins bring persistent vomiting and diarrhoea, worst in children — rarely dangerous to an adult, reliably miserable, and enough of them will land you on a drip.

lookalikes.name: Black nightshade and bittersweet nightshade (Solanum ptycanthum / S. americanum, S. dulcamara)
lookalikes.tell: Not shrubs. Both are weeds of dune parking lots, path edges, blowouts and disturbed back-dune sand, and both fruit right through beach plum season. Pull one and it lifts out of the sand on a soft green stem with a shallow root, where a beach plum is anchored woody. Black nightshade: shiny black berries about 1/4 in in small drooping umbel-like clusters off the side of the stem, thin shiny skin with no waxy bloom; the unripe green ones carry the most solanine and are the ones that poison people. Bittersweet nightshade: a scrambling vine with purple star-shaped flowers, leaves often with two small lobes at the base, and egg-shaped berries that ripen green to yellow to bright translucent red in clusters. In the bucket, either one is obvious the moment you cut it: soft tomato-like pulp full of many tiny flat seeds, and no stone at all.

lookalikes.name: Poison ivy (Toxicodendron radicans)
lookalikes.tell: Not a fruit lookalike — the plant you will actually put your hands and forearms into. It is the most abundant thing sharing dune thickets with beach plum, growing as a low shrubby clump in open sand as readily as a hairy-stemmed vine climbing up through the plum bushes, and by September its leaves have turned brilliant scarlet, which a beginner reads as autumn colour rather than a warning. Three leaflets, the middle one on a distinctly longer stalk, margins irregularly toothed or lobed; the fruit is a cluster of dull white to tan waxy drupes in the leaf axils, persisting all winter, which is also the easiest way to spot the bare stems in a thicket in early spring. Urushiol is in every part including leafless winter stems and roots, transfers off clothing, buckets, knives and dog fur for months, and is aerosolised if dune brush is burned. Long sleeves, and wash the tools and the clothes.

lookalikes.name: Bayberry (Morella pensylvanica, syn. Myrica pensylvanica)
lookalikes.tell: The shrub beach plum most often stands shoulder to shoulder with, and the commonest harmless mix-up on the dune. Fruit is a hard grey-white waxy bead about 1/8 in, packed tight against last year's wood in short clusters, and it stays on the bush all winter — nothing like a plum in the hand, but a knee-high grey-fruited dune shrub reads as 'beach plum' to somebody who has seen neither. Crush a leaf: bayberry is strongly aromatic, resinous and spicy, and the leaves are semi-evergreen, leathery, untoothed or with a few teeth near the tip. Beach plum leaves smell of very little. Bayberry wax makes candles, not jam.

lookalikes.name: Other wild plums — American, Canada, Chickasaw, flatwoods and sloe (Prunus americana, P. nigra, P. angustifolia, P. umbellata, P. spinosa)
lookalikes.tell: These are true plums, edible in the flesh exactly as beach plum is, so this particular group of mix-ups costs you flavour rather than health — the deadly members of the genus are listed separately above. Beach plum is a low, mounded, wind-sheared shrub, usually knee to shoulder high (to 6–8 ft only in shelter), rooted in loose sand within sight of salt water and spreading in root-suckering clones. American and Canada plum are upright thicket-forming shrubs or small trees of inland fencerows and river terraces, with thorny branchlets and larger fruit; Chickasaw and flatwoods plum replace them south of the Delmarva, outside this plant's range. Be honest about sloe (P. spinosa), naturalised in coastal New England: it is not reliably separable from beach plum on fruit alone, and the usual advice to look for thorns fails in both directions, since old beach plum spur shoots go stiff and stubby. Sloe is fiercely thorny, its fruit is smaller, harder and more astringent, and it also makes excellent jelly — so if you cannot split them, cook them and stop worrying. One rule covers the whole genus and is not optional: the stone is cyanogenic in every species here. Eat the flesh, discard the stones, never grind them.

harvest: The plant is tougher than the ground it stands on. Dune faces are held together by beachgrass roots and a footpath through one is the damage — stay on boardwalks, established blowout paths and the wrack line, and work the thickets from the landward side. Pick by hand, fruit by fruit. The single most common injury foragers do to beach plum is snapping or bending branches down to strip them, and because the fruit is borne on short spur shoots on older wood, a broken branch is several seasons of crop, not one. Do not rake, beat or comb the bushes, and never dig one up — transplanted wild beach plums almost always die, and nursery stock is cheap. Leave a real share on every bush: recruitment on developed shorelines is poor, and the fruit feeds migrating birds through exactly these weeks. In Maine, take nothing. The Maine Natural Areas Program lists Prunus maritima as state Endangered (S1), documented in 11 towns across Cumberland, Knox, Sagadahoc and York counties, with beachfront development having cut an already small range and populations that are small to begin with. In eastern Connecticut, leave any odd round-leaved dwarf beach plum alone — that is Graves' beach plum, var. gravesii, one of the rarest plants in the region. Access is the other half of it: most dune land is town conservation land, state park, national seashore, national wildlife refuge, land trust or private with a sign on it, and the rules are not uniform. National Park Service units set their own terms in the Superintendent's Compendium — some designate hand-picking of fruit for personal use, some prohibit collecting entirely — and refuges generally require that gathering be explicitly allowed. Check the specific unit before you go, and get permission on private land, which on a barrier beach is most land. Two practical hazards: late-season shorebird and tern closures can still be in force into August, so respect symbolic fencing even where it looks abandoned, and dune thickets are heavy tick ground in late summer — tuck in, treat clothing, and check the same evening. Skip bushes on road shoulders that get right-of-way herbicide, and bushes immediately below sprayed and fertilised beachfront lawns.

name: Glasswort (sea beans, pickleweed)
scientific: Salicornia spp. — the annuals S. depressa and S. maritima on the northern Atlantic coast, S. bigelovii on the Atlantic and Gulf, and S. rubra and S. utahensis on inland alkaline flats; the perennials S. ambigua (woody glasswort) on the southeastern and Gulf coast and S. pacifica on the Pacific. Sarcocornia has been folded into Salicornia on phylogenetic evidence, so Sarcocornia pacifica and Sarcocornia ambigua in older books are these same plants under an abandoned genus. Treat 'Salicornia virginica' as a dead name: its type specimen is an annual, and the name was misapplied for a century to both the Atlantic and the Pacific perennials, so a label reading S. virginica tells you nothing about which plant is in front of you. Nothing in the genus is toxic — every Salicornia in North America is edible, and the danger in this entry is entirely about what else is standing in the marsh with it.
habitat: Full sun, no canopy at all. Glasswort is a plant of bare, wet, hyper-saline mineral ground — places where salt has chemically removed the competition and left open mud that nothing else will colonise. On the Atlantic and Gulf it is the pioneer on soft unvegetated tidal silt: the seaward fringe below the smooth cordgrass band (Sporobolus alterniflorus, long known as Spartina alterniflora), the raw cut banks of tidal creeks and ditch spoil, and above all the salt pannes — shallow, poorly drained bald spots inside the high marsh where tide water ponds and evaporates until the soil runs saltier than seawater, ringed by salt-meadow cordgrass (Spartina patens), saltgrass (Distichlis spicata) and sea lavender. On the Pacific the perennial S. pacifica carpets the middle marsh in a dense low mat from San Diego to Puget Sound, interwoven with saltgrass, Jaumea carnosa, alkali heath (Frankenia salina) and — this matters — arrowgrass. Inland, the same genus turns up hundreds of miles from any ocean on the drying margins of alkaline playas, salt lakes and alkali seeps: the Great Salt Lake shoreline and the Great Basin, Nevada and Wyoming alkali flats, the Oklahoma salt plains, and scattered saline lakes and springs on the northern plains. That inland occurrence is real but patchy and it follows the salt, not the map — do not go looking for glasswort in ordinary midwestern wetland. Soil is fine silt or clay, waterlogged and anoxic, neutral on the coast and strongly alkaline inland; the plant will not grow in shade and will not persist where fresh water has diluted the salt out. One thing to know about the ground rather than the plant: the brackish upper edge of these marshes — the ditch heads, creek tops and freshwater seeps where the salt runs out — is prime water hemlock ground on both coasts and inland, and you will walk through it to reach the pannes.
indicator: A salt panne: a bare, glistening, hard-baked bald spot inside an otherwise grassy high marsh, ringed by salt-meadow cordgrass and saltgrass, with nothing growing on it but low succulent stems. Inland, the equivalent signal is a white alkali crust at the rim of a playa under greasewood and shadscale.
parts:
Only the tender new upper growth — the top two to four inches of a stem, taken where it snaps off with a wet click rather than bending or stringing. Squeeze before you pick: firm and juicy is worth taking, and anything that flexes has already gone woody. Every Salicornia lays down a tough central fibrous strand as it matures, and on the perennials (S. pacifica on the Pacific, S. ambigua on the Gulf and southeast) that strand is present in all but the freshest tips; those are still good if you draw the flesh off between your teeth and discard the string, artichoke-leaf style. Colour is a clock, not a warning — green is prime, and the orange-red flush that takes the whole plant as the season closes means woody and bitter, not poisonous. Season runs earliest in the south: March to May on the Gulf, in Florida and in southern California, roughly May to July on the mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest, and June to August only in Maine and on the inland alkali flats, where the annuals germinate late.

Nothing about glasswort requires cooking to make it safe; it is eaten raw in the countries that eat the most of it. What it requires is fresh water and restraint. Rinse hard in several changes of cold fresh water — you are washing off tidal silt and whatever came in on the last tide, and marsh mud in a raw salad is the realistic way this plant makes someone ill. A 30–60 second blanch in unsalted boiling water followed straight into an ice bath sets the colour, softens the skin and pulls out a meaningful share of the salt; a second change of blanching water pulls out more. Never salt the pan, the brine, or anything it goes into: the tissue can run several percent sodium by fresh weight, and a generous helping can account for an adult's entire daily sodium on its own, which is a real problem on a sodium-restricted diet or on blood-pressure medication. Salicornia also contains oxalic acid. That has never been an issue at culinary quantities, but it is another reason this is a side dish and not a salad base, and anyone with a history of calcium-oxalate kidney stones should treat it the way they treat spinach. Standard uses: small amounts raw, blanched and dressed, flashed in a hot dry pan for under a minute, or brined and pickled — the oldest treatment, and where pickled samphire comes from.

lookalikes.name: Seaside and marsh arrowgrass (Triglochin maritima, T. palustris, T. concinna, T. striata)
lookalikes.tell: Rooted in the same salt pannes and brackish flats, routinely growing up through the glasswort itself. The structural difference is absolute: arrowgrass has leaves, Salicornia has none. Arrowgrass leaves rise in a basal tuft from one short rootstock — fleshy, dark green, 6–18 in, half-round in cross-section (flat or grooved on one face, rounded on the other), unjointed, solid, tapering to a point, wrapped at the base in a papery sheath. Glasswort has no leaves and no basal tuft: one round succulent stem branching in opposite pairs from ground level, visibly swollen and constricted at every joint, snapping cleanly at a joint with a crisp wet pop. CRITICAL SEASONAL FAILURE: the standard 'obviously jointed and segmented' tell is at its weakest exactly when it matters most. The youngest unbranched Salicornia shoots in April and May are slim green spikes with barely-marked joints, and that is precisely when triglochinin peaks in new arrowgrass growth. On anything under about three inches, do not judge by outline — roll the stem between finger and thumb (glasswort is round and evenly plump all the way around; an arrowgrass blade has one flat or grooved face you can feel), and pull one plant to check the base for a tuft and a papery collar. Do not wait for the flower spike either: the long naked stalk of small green flowers ripening to golden-brown fruit is absent or immature through much of sea-bean season, and it is no use at all for the vegetative material actually going in your bag. Toxicity: the green leaves carry the cyanogenic glycosides triglochinin and taxiphyllin, which release hydrogen cyanide when the tissue is crushed or chewed. USDA's Poisonous Plant Research Laboratory puts the lethal dose at a quarter-pound to three pounds of stunted arrowgrass for a 600 lb animal, eaten at once; scaled to human size that puts a few hundred grams squarely in the dangerous range. Cyanide poisoning moves in minutes to an hour — rapid breathing, weakness, convulsions, death. Levels run highest in drought-stressed, frost-hit or regrowing plants, which describes the stressed panne edge glasswort favours. Arrowgrass appears in some foraging books as an edible in gram quantities; that is not permission to fill a bag with it by accident.

lookalikes.name: Water hemlock (Cicuta maculata, C. douglasii, C. bulbifera)
lookalikes.tell: Listed here not because it resembles glasswort — it does not, in any way — but because it owns the ground you cross to reach the pannes, and it is the most acutely lethal plant in North America. It occupies the brackish and freshwater upper margins of tidal marshes on both coasts, ditch heads, creek tops and alkali seeps inland, and the mistake it causes is the beginner who comes home from a sea-bean trip with 'some other green from the same spot.' It is a 3–8 ft umbellifer: doubly or triply compound leaves, umbrella-shaped clusters of small white flowers, a stout hollow stem often streaked or mottled purple at the base, and a chambered rootstock that weeps yellow resinous fluid when cut. The leaf tell that works in the season you are out there: the veins in each toothed leaflet run to the NOTCHES between the teeth, not to the tips. Check several leaflets rather than one — the character is generally reliable but not perfectly consistent leaflet to leaflet, and it is a confirmation, never a clearance. Cicutoxin brings violent seizures within 15–60 minutes and a single mouthful of root has killed adults. Nothing about glasswort is compound, leafy, umbelled, hollow or purple-streaked; if what you are holding has a leaf on it, it is not a sea bean.

lookalikes.name: Halogeton / saltlover (Halogeton glomeratus)
lookalikes.tell: Inland only, and it is on the exact ground the inland glassworts (S. rubra, S. utahensis) grow on: alkaline playa margins, salt flats, saline roadsides and disturbed alkali soil through the Great Basin and Intermountain West. It is fleshy and blue-green flushing red, just like glasswort, but it HAS LEAVES — alternate, sausage-shaped, 3–20 mm, each tipped with a fine bristle that is easy to overlook by eye and impossible to miss by touch (running a fingertip up the plant is the fastest field check you have), with a tuft of white wool in each leaf axil, borne on ordinary round unjointed stems that build a rounded bush 6–18 in across. Glasswort has no leaves, no axillary wool, no bristle tips, and carries a swollen node every half inch or so. Toxicity: 30–40% soluble sodium oxalate by dry weight, with individual plants recorded near 28%. Twelve to eighteen ounces kills a sheep; it killed sheep in the thousands across the western range through the 1940s and 50s. Soluble oxalate strips calcium out of the blood and destroys the kidneys — tetany, coma, renal failure, and lasting kidney damage in survivors. Russian thistle (Salsola tragus) seedlings share the same ground and are also fleshy and spine-tipped; they are not glasswort either. The jointed, leafless stem is the character that decides, never succulence and never the salt-flat habitat, which all of these share.

lookalikes.name: Greasewood (Sarcobatus vermiculatus)
lookalikes.tell: The shrub standing over inland glasswort flats through the Great Basin and northern plains — you will brush past it reaching for the good stuff, and its bright fleshy shoot tips look pickable. It is a spiny woody shrub 3–8 ft tall with white to pale grey bark and alternate, bright green, fleshy LINEAR leaves roughly 1–4 cm long on unjointed woody twigs. Glasswort inland is a soft low herb under about a foot with no leaves at all and no woody grey stem. The leaves carry soluble sodium and potassium oxalates; roughly 1 g oxalate per kg body weight is lethal in sheep, about half a kilo of green leaf, with the same hypocalcaemia and kidney failure as halogeton. Concentration climbs through the growing season and peaks late summer into fall — the back half of glasswort season, not the start of it. Useful the other way round as well: a greasewood flat is a reliable sign you are on the right kind of ground for inland glasswort.

lookalikes.name: Horsetail and scouring rush (Equisetum arvense, E. hyemale, E. variegatum, E. palustre and relatives)
lookalikes.tell: The only plant in this habitat that genuinely shares glasswort's key character — jointed, segmented, leafless green stems — which means the tell most books give for Salicornia describes horsetail just as well. It grows at the freshwater and brackish margins of the same estuaries, in dune slacks, on ditch banks and in seepy upper-marsh edges, sometimes within yards of the sea-bean patch. Three checks, all working on vegetative material in season: (1) Texture — run it between your fingers. Horsetail is harsh and gritty with silica and finely ridged lengthwise; glasswort is smooth, slick and plump. (2) The node — horsetail carries a distinct collar of tiny fused, often black-tipped teeth at each joint, and frequently a whorl of thin branches radiating from it; a glasswort node is a bare swelling with at most two opposite scale points and one opposite branch. (3) Snap it — horsetail is hollow, dry and hard-fibrous; glasswort is solid, wet and squeaks against the teeth. Horsetail is also not salty, but confirm identity before tasting anything, not the other way round. Toxicity: thiaminase destroys vitamin B1, and E. palustre additionally carries the alkaloid palustrine. This is a cumulative injury rather than a same-day emergency like arrowgrass — thiamine-deficiency neurological disease is well documented in livestock, and it is why horsetail preparations sold for human use carry dosing limits — but it is not food and it does not belong in the bag.

lookalikes.name: Sea blite and seepweed (Suaeda spp., including annual seablite)
lookalikes.tell: Grows shoulder to shoulder with glasswort in the same coastal pannes and on the same inland alkali flats, is equally fleshy, and flushes the same red late in the season, so it gets picked by mistake constantly. It has obvious leaves: narrow, linear to awl-shaped, half-round fleshy leaves 1–5 cm long set alternately all the way up a slender unjointed stem. No joints, no swollen nodes, and it will not snap at a segment because it has none. Not dangerous — Suaeda is itself eaten in several cuisines — but it is tougher, more bitter, and can run high in nitrate and oxalate on saline ground, and it is not what a sea-bean recipe is asking for.

lookalikes.name: Iodinebush, also called pickleweed (Allenrolfea occidentalis)
lookalikes.tell: The inland one that catches people on the name alone: it is jointed, leafless and succulent, and 'pickleweed' is applied to both plants across the Great Basin and Southwest. Allenrolfea is a woody, densely branched shrub 1–5 ft tall with a grey woody trunk and short plump jointed green branchlets only at the tips; the inland glassworts (S. rubra, S. utahensis) are soft annuals under about a foot with no woody trunk anywhere. Not toxic — the seeds were traditionally gathered and eaten — but the branchlets are bitter, resinous and tough. The woody grey base settles it at a glance, before you get close enough to argue about joints.

harvest:
Pinch or snip the top few inches and leave the plant rooted; never pull it up. This matters more than the usual pick-lightly advice because most of the range's plants are annuals — S. depressa, S. bigelovii, S. maritima, S. rubra all set seed once and die, so a plant stripped before it flowers takes next year's stand off that panne with it. Take the top third at most, from scattered plants, and leave whole patches untouched to seed. The perennials (S. pacifica, S. ambigua) regrow from the base and tolerate tip-picking better, but they are also the ones holding the marsh together. Nothing here justifies a rake, a knife dragged through a stand, or a sack.

Where you walk does more damage than what you cut. Salt marsh peat compacts and does not spring back; a boot trail across a panne becomes a drainage channel, then a bare scar that persists for years. Stay on creek banks, existing paths and firm edges.

Choosing the marsh is a food-safety decision, not just an ethical one. Halophytes are used deliberately for phytoremediation precisely because they take up and concentrate zinc, copper, iron, cadmium and lead out of sediment, and Salicornia is among the plants studied for it. Skip any marsh below a storm drain, marina, boatyard, wastewater outfall, dredge-spoil site, highway or industrial waterfront. State shellfish-closure maps are the best free proxy anyone has for how dirty a given estuary's water is — read them before you pick. On the Gulf and southern Atlantic in summer, do not wade or handle marsh mud with open cuts; warm brackish water is Vibrio country.

A great deal of this plant is legally off limits. Most US salt marsh sits inside national wildlife refuges, national estuarine research reserves, state wildlife management areas or coastal wetland protection acts, where plant collection is usually prohibited outright or permitted only in writing. On the Pacific, pickleweed marsh is the entire habitat of the endangered salt marsh harvest mouse in San Francisco Bay and nesting cover for the California Ridgway's rail; in the Northwest, commercial sea-asparagus harvest is regulated. Find out who owns the marsh and what its rules are before you cut anything.
