name: Staghorn Sumac
scientific: Rhus typhina (syn. R. hirta). Where its range meets smooth sumac the two hybridise freely as R. x pulvinata, with thinly hairy twigs - both parents and the hybrid are used identically. THIS ENTRY COVERS THE PINNATE-LEAVED SUMACS ONLY: staghorn, the hybrid, smooth sumac (R. glabra) and winged or shining sumac (R. copallinum). Those three give the same drink and the same spice and between them cover the parts of the country staghorn does not reach. Every test in this entry - an erect terminal cone, a long pinnate row of 11-31 leaflets, velvet or smooth twigs - assumes that pinnate leaf and fails without it. The three-leaflet sumacs, fragrant sumac (R. aromatica) and skunkbush (R. trilobata, formerly treated as varieties of R. aromatica), are DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED. Their fruit is also a red hairy drupe and is also drunk, but a trifoliolate shrub carries the poison-ivy silhouette, and nothing in this entry's identification set separates the two - so this guide will not send you at one. If you want them, they need their own key and their own tells; the poison ivy lookalike below sets out what would have to be proved first.
habitat: Dry, sunny, sharply drained ground that was disturbed once and then left alone - road cuts, rail embankments, gravel fill, quarry lips, powerline corridors, old pasture and hayfield going back to brush, and the sunny outer edge of a woodlot. It is a pioneer: it will not hold under closed canopy and it will not sit in saturated soil, but it takes thin, rocky, nutrient-poor ground where little else starts, and it runs from root suckers into a clone - dozens to hundreds of stems, one plant, flat-topped, tallest in the middle. Native from Nova Scotia and Quebec west to Ontario and Minnesota, south to Iowa and Indiana and down the Appalachians to northern Georgia. In the southeast it is a mountain and upper-piedmont plant, essentially absent from the coastal plain and the Deep South, where winged and smooth sumac take its place; in the Mountain West and on the Pacific coast it is a planted ornamental and its escapes rather than a wild plant, and the pinnate sumac that actually grows wild out there is smooth sumac (R. glabra), which reaches all the lower 48. Skunkbush (R. trilobata) is the other western Rhus and is often named as the local substitute, but it has three leaflets, not a pinnate row, and this entry does not cover it - see the scientific note and the poison ivy lookalike. One caveat outweighs all of the range detail: NC State lists stream and swamp margins among staghorn's own native habitats, and deadly poison sumac turns up in roadside ditches, powerline corridors, cut-over swamps and seepage slopes. Wet ground does not rule out staghorn, and dry ground does not rule out poison sumac. Never let the ground you are standing on make the identification for you.
indicator: A thicket of thick, forking, felt-covered twigs like antlers in velvet, flat-topped, on a south-facing road cut or rail bank with black locust, eastern redcedar, gray birch, black cherry, goldenrod and little bluestem. Out of season, find the patch by last year's fruit: blackened dark-maroon cones still standing upright over a leafless clone in March mark a female colony worth returning to in July.
parts: The dense upright cone-shaped fruit clusters ('bobs') of the pinnate-leaved sumacs only - staghorn, smooth, winged, and the staghorn-smooth hybrid. Take them when the whole cone is deep rust-red and the hairs still taste sharply sour - lick one before you cut anything, because a cone that tastes of nothing has been rained out and is not worth carrying home. That lick confirms ripeness on a clone you have ALREADY identified; it is never how you identify one. The plant is dioecious; only female clones fruit. The acid sits in the fine hairs on the outside of each drupe, not in the pulp or the seed, so all the flavour is on the surface and cold water is all you need: bruise the cones, cover with COLD water, steep 20 minutes to 4 hours or overnight in the fridge, and strain. Never boil and never use hot water - MSU Extension notes hot water destroys the vitamin C, and it also pulls bitter tannin out of the seeds and stems. Strain twice, the second time through a coffee filter, jelly bag or four layers of muslin; the point is not clarity but removing the fine hairs, which scratch the throat. Do not rinse the cones first - you would be washing off the thing you came for. Whole dried cones keep a year in paper; rub the drupes off the stems and grind coarsely, sieving out the hard seeds, for the tart purple-red spice of za'atar and fattoush. Two safety notes on preparation. Sumac is in the cashew family with mango, pistachio and cashew: people with those allergies, or with strong urushiol sensitivity, occasionally react to edible sumac, so drink no more than 4 oz (120 ml) the first time and wait a full 24 hours before making a pitcher or pouring it for anyone else. And reject any cone that is matted, blackened at the core, webbed with insect frass or dusted with mould - sumac heads hold water and go mouldy after a wet spell.

lookalikes.name: Poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix)
lookalikes.tell: The tells that matter are on the fruit, because the fruit is what you are picking. STAGHORN: a dense, tight, ERECT cone of fuzzy crimson-to-rust drupes at the tip of the twig, standing above the leaves; 11-31 leaflets, every one sharply saw-toothed; young twigs and leaf stalks under dense velvet hair. POISON SUMAC: a loose, open, DANGLING panicle of smooth round yellowish-white to grey-white drupes hanging from the leaf axils along the stem - never a cone, never upright; 7-13 leaflets with entire untoothed margins; every surface hairless. Both hold their fruit into winter, staghorn's dark maroon and erect, poison sumac's dirty white and drooping, so these tells work through the whole harvest season and past it. THREE PUBLISHED TELLS THAT DO NOT WORK. (1) 'It only grows in standing water.' It is a wetland plant, but it is recorded from streamhead pocosins, sandhill seepage bogs, wet thickets, cut-over swamps, powerline corridors and roadside ditches, and Coastal Plain seepage ground is routinely dry at the surface in late summer and autumn - exactly when you are out picking. NC State in turn lists stream and swamp margins for staghorn. Habitat narrows the odds; it never decides. (2) 'Red stalks mean poison sumac.' Its rachis is bright red, but staghorn's petioles and rachis are frequently red too. (3) 'Fuzzy is safe, smooth is poison.' Smooth sumac (R. glabra) is completely hairless and completely edible, and winged sumac (R. copallinum) has untoothed leaflets - absence of fuzz and absence of teeth prove nothing on their own. Leaflet counts overlap at 9-13, so do not count and stop. What proves staghorn is the positive set together: velvet twigs, saw-toothed leaflets, erect red cone. NC State rates poison sumac's poison severity high and states all parts are poisonous; it carries urushiol at higher concentration than poison ivy. Skin contact means severe blistering dermatitis. Getting it into the mouth and throat - precisely what steeping the wrong fruit and drinking it does - risks swelling of the airway, and smoke from burning the plant causes life-threatening lung injury. Never test-taste an unknown sumac. If one cluster in a thicket makes you hesitate, leave the whole clone.

lookalikes.name: Poison ivy and poison oak (Toxicodendron radicans, T. rydbergii, T. pubescens)
lookalikes.tell: Not a confusion with the cone - a confusion with what your arms are in. Poison ivy climbs sumac clones and old-field edges by the yard, and cutting cones means reaching through it. STATE THE LEAFLET RULE IN THE DIRECTION THAT IS ACTUALLY SAFE. Poison ivy and poison oak always carry exactly THREE leaflets on one common stalk, so a pinnate row of nine or more leaflets is never Toxicodendron. THE REVERSE DOES NOT HOLD: three leaflets does not prove poison ivy, and it certainly does not prove anything edible - it only proves you are not holding a sumac this entry covers. Anything trifoliolate stops here. WHY THIS NEEDS SAYING: fragrant sumac (R. aromatica) and skunkbush (R. trilobata) are three-leaflet Rhus with red hairy fruit that people genuinely drink, and they are the reason a bare 'three leaflets, leave it' rule gets argued with. This guide excludes them rather than key them from a screen. If you are standing in front of a three-leaflet shrub regardless, these are the tells that separate a harmless Rhus from Toxicodendron, and ALL THREE must agree before it is anything other than poison ivy. (1) MIDDLE LEAFLET STALK - Missouri Department of Conservation: poison ivy's terminal leaflet sits on its own stalk 1/2 to 1 3/4 inches long, standing the middle leaflet well out past the two side ones; fragrant sumac's terminal leaflet is sessile or on a stalk of a few millimetres, seated almost directly between its neighbours, and skunkbush is the same. (2) FRUIT - fragrant sumac and skunkbush carry small RED, HAIRY, often sticky drupes packed in a short tight cluster AT THE BRANCH TIP, ripening June to August; poison ivy and poison oak carry smooth, waxy, HAIRLESS, greyish-white to cream drupes in loose open clusters hanging FROM THE LEAF AXILS along the stem, ripening August to November. Red and fuzzy at the tip against white and smooth at the joint. (3) HABIT - poison ivy climbs, sending woody vines shaggy with dense aerial rootlets up sumac trunks and fence posts; fragrant sumac and skunkbush never climb at all, and hold as low spreading shrubs. Two things that are NOT on that list. Do not use the crush-and-smell test - fragrant sumac is named for its scent, but crushing a doubtful leaf is precisely how urushiol gets onto your hands. And do not lean on glossiness: poison ivy is often shiny and the Rhus leaves duller, but new growth and dry weather ruin that. Look before you touch. In the West, where skunkbush replaces fragrant sumac, the plant on the other side of the same test is Pacific poison oak (T. diversilobum) - also trifoliolate, also white axillary fruit. Whichever plant you settle on, the urushiol rules do not change: it is the same oil as poison sumac, generally milder, and it transfers off pruners, gloves, boot laces and the bag you carried the cones in for a year or more. If you contact it, wash the skin with cool water and a degreasing soap or urushiol-specific cleanser as soon as you can - WITHIN ABOUT 30 MINUTES TO 2 HOURS is when washing does the most good - and wash the tools and the picking clothes separately from everything else, not just your hands. Never burn any of it: urushiol in smoke reaches the lungs and those cases are emergencies.

lookalikes.name: Tree-of-heaven (Ailanthus altissima)
lookalikes.tell: The commonest thing mistaken for sumac in the East, and in August and September its fruit is rosy-red: flat, twisted, papery samaras (winged seeds) in big DROOPING clusters that fade to tan, against staghorn's dense upright cone of fuzzy drupes. Squeeze one - a samara is dry paper around a single central seed, a sumac drupe is a fuzzy bead. Leaflets are entire except for one or two glandular teeth at the very base, each with a bump-like gland underneath; staghorn is toothed the whole length of every leaflet. Crushed Ailanthus foliage smells rank, like rancid peanut butter or burnt nuts; sumac smells green and resinous. Twigs are stout, smooth and hairless with huge heart-shaped leaf scars - no velvet anywhere - and the bark is smooth grey with pale striping against staghorn's rough brown. It contains ailanthone; the sap causes contact dermatitis and myocarditis has been reported after ingesting bark preparations. Nothing on it is food. It is also the tree spotted lanternfly swarms, so a red-clustered 'sumac' crawling with lanternflies is Ailanthus.

lookalikes.name: Red elderberry (Sambucus racemosa)
lookalikes.tell: Bright red fruit held UP in a rounded or pyramidal cluster at the branch tips, in the same edges, clearings and old fields, ripening June to July in the north, around the Great Lakes and at elevation - which overlaps the front of the sumac season. The berries are juicy and squash between your fingers, sitting loose in an open branching cluster; sumac drupes are dry, fuzzy and packed shoulder to shoulder into a solid cone you could hold like a torch. Leaves are OPPOSITE on the stem (staghorn is alternate) with 5-7 leaflets, and the stems are soft with thick white pith you can push out with a twig. Raw fruit, seeds, leaves, bark and stems carry cyanogenic glycosides - nausea, vomiting, cramps and diarrhoea from a handful raw. Do not transfer the reputation of common elderberry to this: black-fruited S. canadensis has a flat-topped cluster and purple-black fruit and is a different plant.

harvest: Cut cones with pruners instead of snapping them; a torn twig tip takes out next year's fruiting wood on that branch. The timing that matters is weather, not calendar: the acid is on the outside of the drupes and rain rinses it off, so pick after three or four dry days and before the next rain, and taste one cone from every clone before you cut - as a ripeness check on a clone already identified, never as the identification itself. Ripening runs early to mid July in the southern Appalachians, late July to mid August in Pennsylvania and the Midwest, and mid August into September in northern New England, Michigan and Ontario; cones stay usable through October and, in a dry autumn, into November. Fruit still hanging in winter is worth much less to you and much more to everything else - the cones are classic late-winter emergency food for robins, bluebirds, cardinals, catbirds, grouse and turkey when nothing else is left - so take your share in summer and leave the winter fruit alone. Sumac is abundant and clonal and does not need protecting the way ramps do, but a clone is one genetic plant, so stripping 'just this bush' can strip a hundred stems' worth of fruit from a single individual; a few cones per clone is invisible to it. Site is a bigger question than quantity. Road cuts, rail banks and powerline corridors are exactly where sumac thrives and exactly where herbicide is sprayed on a schedule - skip them, and skip the first thirty feet of any road shoulder for salt and exhaust. Ask before cutting on land you do not own, and check land-manager rules: many state parks and all National Park Service units restrict or prohibit plant collection.
